executive_summary: Today's intelligence picture is dominated by two converging pressures: an active U.S.-Iran conflict that is simultaneously straining allied cohesion, consuming Pentagon resources at an accelerating pace, and exposing underappreciated vulnerabilities in global oil markets, while adversaries are exploiting the distraction to advance asymmetric campaigns across cyber and physical infrastructure. The ICS and cyber sections tell a related story, with a 51% spike in OT and IoT vulnerabilities, active exploitation of critical industrial control systems, and Russian GRU use of compromised IP cameras to surveil European and Ukrainian infrastructure, suggesting that state and state-aligned actors are actively probing the soft underbelly of Western critical infrastructure during a period of military and political stress. Taiwan's deliberate mobile network throttling during Han Kuang exercises and Chinese military doctrine explicitly targeting Taiwan's will to fight rather than just its defenses are a notable pairing, indicating Taipei is rehearsing for exactly the kind of gray-zone degradation Beijing is preparing to impose. The thread connecting all four sections is systemic overextension: the U.S. is fiscally and diplomatically stretched by the Iran conflict, allies from Seoul to Paris are signaling doubt, adversaries from Moscow to Beijing are probing for exploitable gaps, and domestic oversight mechanisms from TSA cybersecurity roadmaps to Pentagon budget processes are flagging as inadequate to the current threat tempo

sections.title: Cyber
sections.intro: Today's cyber landscape is dominated by a wave of ICS/OT vulnerability disclosures and actively exploited flaws, alongside a notable consumer privacy enforcement action and a smart TV supply chain transparency issue.

items.headline: CISA flags four vulnerabilities under active exploitation, including legacy router flaw and AI platform code execution risk
items.summary: CISA added four CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, including a 2021 stack-based buffer overflow in DD-WRT routers and a 2026 code-inclusion flaw in Langflow, an AI workflow platform. Active exploitation of these vulnerabilities means federal agencies face binding patching deadlines, but the broader risk extends to enterprises using these products. The Langflow flaw is particularly notable given the rapid adoption of AI development tools with limited security vetting.

items.headline: Rockwell Automation ICS products hit with multiple critical vulnerabilities spanning denial-of-service to arbitrary code execution
items.summary: CISA issued three separate advisories covering Rockwell Automation products — POINT I/O, Ex I/O, and Studio 5000 Logix Designer — exposing industrial control systems to denial-of-service attacks and, in Logix Designer's case, arbitrary code execution and configuration tampering. These products are widely deployed in manufacturing and critical infrastructure environments, raising the operational risk profile significantly. OT security teams should prioritize patch assessment given Rockwell's central role in U.S. industrial automation.

items.headline: LG moves to ban smart TV apps that silently route user traffic as residential proxies
items.summary: LG announced it will suspend webOS apps that convert users' televisions into residential proxy nodes, following researcher findings that over 42% of apps in its store enabled third-party traffic routing without user awareness. This practice is commercially exploited by proxy networks to obscure malicious or fraudulent internet traffic, making unwitting TV owners complicit in abuse. The move sets a precedent for smart TV platform governance, but enforcement credibility will depend on how rigorously LG audits existing and future submissions.

items.headline: Spain fines bankrupt 23andMe nearly $3 million over security failures that enabled 2023 mass data breach
items.summary: Spain's data protection authority levied a €2.8 million fine against 23andMe, citing cybersecurity deficiencies that allowed the 2023 credential-stuffing breach affecting 6.9 million users globally, including over 2,600 Spanish nationals. The fine adds to the company's mounting legal and financial liabilities as it navigates bankruptcy proceedings, raising questions about the practical recoverability of penalties against insolvent data custodians. Regulators across the EU are watching this case as a test of GDPR enforcement against collapsed companies holding sensitive genomic data.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

sections.title: Geopolitical
sections.intro: Global fault lines are deepening across multiple theaters, with China expanding its Taiwan warfare doctrine, Ukraine pressing its drone campaign into Russian territory, and the U.S.-Iran war reverberating through key allied relationships worldwide.

items.headline: Chinese Military Doctrine Targets Taiwan's Will to Fight, Not Just Its Defenses
items.summary: Restricted PLA research documents outline a strategy to defeat Taipei by collapsing civilian and military cognitive cohesion—blocking external aid, dismantling operational systems, and eliminating recovery capacity rather than relying solely on kinetic force. This signals Beijing is developing a hybrid warfare model that treats psychological and informational degradation as decisive war-winning tools alongside conventional operations. Watch for how Taiwan and U.S. planners adapt deterrence frameworks to account for this population-targeting approach.

items.headline: Ukraine's Deep-Strike Drone Campaign Is Shifting War's Momentum Against Russia
items.summary: Ukraine's expanded long-range drone operations are degrading Russian logistics, energy infrastructure, and operational planning deeper inside Russian territory than at any prior point in the conflict. The strikes create compounding pressure on Moscow's rear-area sustainment—but Russia's adaptation capacity and escalation calculus remain key variables. The central question is whether Ukraine can convert tactical disruption into durable strategic leverage before battlefield attrition undermines its position.

items.headline: U.S.-Iran War Is Straining Allied Relationships from Seoul to Paris
items.summary: Five expert assessments reveal that the U.S. military conflict with Iran is producing significant diplomatic friction with South Korea, India, Ukraine, France, and the United Kingdom—each resisting or conditioning their support in distinct ways reflecting their own strategic interests. The divergence exposes the limits of U.S. coalition management when a conflict carries high economic and escalatory risk for partners. These fractures could constrain future U.S. flexibility in both the Middle East and in parallel theaters like the Indo-Pacific.

items.headline: Iran War Exposes Oil Market Vulnerabilities That Washington Is Underestimating
items.summary: Depleted strategic petroleum reserves, altered shipping dynamics around the Strait of Hormuz, and Houthi interdiction activity have left global oil markets far more exposed to price shocks than the Trump administration's posture suggests. Previous assumptions about buffer capacity no longer hold under current conditions, meaning even a modest escalation could trigger disproportionate price spikes. Energy markets and allied governments reliant on stable oil prices should treat this as a near-term systemic risk, not a manageable background variable.

sections.title: Military
sections.intro: The Iran conflict dominates today's military picture, with rising casualty counts, a $67 billion Pentagon funding request, and diplomatic pressure spreading to NATO's eastern flank.

items.headline: Pentagon seeks $67 billion more as Iran war costs top $37.5 billion and casualties mount
items.summary: Defense Secretary Hegseth told senators the conflict with Iran has cost $37.5 billion to date and submitted a $67.1 billion emergency supplemental funding request. Separately, the Pentagon identified a third soldier killed in an Iranian attack in Jordan — Sgt. Angel Rampersad, 28 — and a fourth soldier, Sgt. Michael Swinton, killed during controlled detonation of an Iranian drone. The compounding human and financial toll will intensify congressional debate over war authority and spending priorities.

items.headline: Iran presses Bulgaria to deny US access to its territory for military operations
items.summary: Iran's foreign ministry warned Bulgaria against permitting American forces to use Bulgarian territory in operations against Iran, signaling Tehran's effort to fracture NATO solidarity and limit US basing options in southeastern Europe. The move reflects a broader Iranian pressure campaign targeting smaller NATO members perceived as more susceptible to coercion. Watch for similar warnings directed at other flank states hosting US logistics or strike assets.

items.headline: USS Charlotte crew honored for role in sinking Iranian frigate during Operation Epic Fury
items.summary: The Navy awarded its Unit Commendation to the crew of the Los Angeles-class submarine USS Charlotte following its reported participation in Operation Epic Fury, which involved sinking an Iranian frigate. The public recognition is notable given submarine operations are rarely acknowledged, suggesting the Navy is deliberately signaling undersea strike capability to Iran and regional partners. The award also underscores the submarine force's central role in the campaign.

items.headline: US lawmakers at Paris Airshow warn Pentagon budget gridlock threatens Golden Dome and allied confidence
items.summary: Senators attending Europe's largest airshow cautioned that funding for the Golden Dome missile defense initiative may fall short this year due to congressional budget paralysis, a message that lands poorly at a moment when US allies are being asked to deepen defense cooperation. The optics of American legislators airing domestic funding failures at an international defense forum underscores the reputational risk of prolonged appropriations uncertainty. The Golden Dome program's timeline and procurement decisions are now a variable to track closely.

sections.title: Intel / OSINT
sections.intro: Today's intelligence picture is shaped by leadership transitions at ODNI, Taiwan stress-testing civilian resilience infrastructure, and opportunistic hackers targeting a sitting head of state.

items.headline: Jay Clayton's ODNI nomination clears Senate Intelligence Committee on party-line vote
items.summary: The Senate Intelligence Committee advanced Clayton's nomination to lead the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, sending it to the full Senate. The party-line vote signals continued partisan friction over intelligence community oversight at a moment when ODNI's coordination role across 18 agencies carries heightened strategic weight. Confirmation on the Senate floor remains the key milestone to watch.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: Taiwan deliberately throttles mobile networks to 1% capacity during Han Kuang resilience exercises
items.summary: As part of its annual Han Kuang civil-military drills, Taiwan is intentionally degrading 4G and 5G networks island-wide to simulate wartime communications disruption. The exercise reveals deliberate thinking about infrastructure fragility under conflict conditions — a direct response to how Russia's invasion exposed Ukraine's communications vulnerabilities. How Taiwan's population and emergency services cope under degraded connectivity is the operational intelligence value being generated here.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

items.headline: Kenyan presidential website defaced with bitcoin ransom demand and data-leak threat
items.summary: Attackers replaced the homepage of President William Ruto's official website with a cryptocurrency wallet address, threatening to release unspecified sensitive information if payment was not made. The incident combines defacement, extortion, and implicit intelligence leverage — a pattern increasingly used against government targets to generate both financial and political pressure. Kenyan authorities have opened an investigation, but the nature of any data potentially exfiltrated remains unconfirmed.
items.source: The Record from Recorded Future News

sections.title: ICS / SCADA / OT
sections.intro: OT and IoT infrastructure face a confluence of rising vulnerabilities, state-sponsored exploitation, and governance gaps that collectively raise the risk profile for critical systems.

items.headline: Forescout Data Shows 51% Spike in Vulnerabilities Hitting IoT and OT Networks
items.summary: Forescout's latest research documents a sharp acceleration in vulnerabilities targeting IoT and OT environments, driven by AI-assisted attacks and increasingly sophisticated supply chain intrusions. The scale of the increase signals that passive asset visibility alone is no longer sufficient — defenders need active exposure management tuned to OT protocols and device constraints. Organizations running legacy industrial hardware with long patch cycles are particularly exposed.

items.headline: Dutch Intelligence Flags Russian GRU Use of Compromised IP Cameras to Surveil European and Ukrainian Infrastructure
items.summary: Dutch security agencies have attributed a systematic campaign of IP camera exploitation to Russian state actors, targeting devices across the Netherlands and other European countries to conduct pre-operational surveillance. Insecure internet-facing cameras on or near critical infrastructure perimeters provide adversaries with physical situational awareness at low cost and risk. Organizations should audit externally visible cameras, enforce credential hygiene, and segment camera networks from OT environments.

items.headline: GAO Finds TSA Cybersecurity Roadmap Outdated, FAA Implementation Falling Short in Aviation Sector
items.summary: A GAO review concludes that the TSA's aviation cyber roadmap has not kept pace with the evolving threat landscape, and that the FAA has failed to fully implement key cybersecurity measures — leaving a critical transportation sector with structural governance gaps. Aviation OT systems, including navigation, air traffic control support, and ground infrastructure, remain at risk if oversight frameworks lag behind attacker capabilities. Congress and the agencies will need to reconcile these findings with near-term remediation timelines.

items.headline: Trump Executive Order Mandates Defense Contractors Map Software and Supplier Cyber Risks End-to-End
items.summary: A new executive order requires defense contractors to build comprehensive visibility into their software dependencies, foreign ownership structures, and supplier-level cyber risks across critical supply chains. For OT-adjacent defense contractors — including those supplying components to weapons systems, energy infrastructure, or communications hardware — this adds a significant compliance burden but also a forcing function for long-overdue SBOM and third-party risk programs. Watch for implementation guidance that may extend requirements deeper into industrial subcontractors.
